subject: korean
title: A 'no' that never says no
goal: Infer from a very short chat that a softened reply declines one day but not the whole plan, point to the evidence, and write your own soft refusal with an alternative.
thinking: Inferring a refusal that is not stated
Separating what is refused (the day) from what is not (the plan)
Producing a softened reply for a classmate
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks what '좀' or '-은/는' means in isolation. Here you decide what a real reply means from the whole chat, justify it with evidence, and then produce your own soft refusal.
prerequisites: Knows basic -아요/어요 endings and day-of-the-week words
material:
Two classmates, 민수 and 수진, text each other. They use polite -요 speech with each other. (😅 = a face with a small sweat drop, an awkward smile.)

민수: 토요일에 영화 볼까요?
수진: 토요일은 좀… 😅
민수: 그럼 일요일은요?
수진: 일요일은 좋아요!

steps.prompt: What does 수진 mean by '토요일은 좀…'?

options.text: Saturday is not good for her; she is declining that day.
Saturday is great for her and she is excited.
options.reveals: '좀…' trailing off with an awkward emoji is a hesitation, not excitement. Look at how the next line (그럼 일요일은요?) reacts.

options.text: She never wants to watch a movie with 민수.
options.reveals: This reads too much into it. Her last line, 일요일은 좋아요!, shows she still wants to go.

options.text: She did not understand the question.
options.reveals: She answers the question directly by naming the day, so she understood it.

steps.explain: '좀…' softens a refusal so that nobody has to say '안 돼요'. The topic marker -은 in '토요일은' singles out Saturday, and 민수 reacts by offering another day.
hints: Read the next line from 민수: how does he react?
Notice that 수진 never says 네 or 아니요. What did she leave unfinished?

steps.prompt: Which pieces of evidence show that 수진 still wants to see the movie? Choose all that apply.

options.text: She answers '일요일은 좋아요!' when 민수 offers Sunday.
She uses the word '좀'.
options.reveals: '좀' softens a refusal; it says nothing about whether she likes the plan.

options.text: She added an emoji.
options.reveals: The emoji shows she feels awkward, not that she wants the movie.

options.text: She said '토요일은', naming only the day, not the movie itself.

steps.explain: She never rejects the movie. She only rejects Saturday (토요일은), and she accepts Sunday.
hints: Find the lines where she says something positive.
Compare what she names in '토요일은 좀…' with what she names in '일요일은 좋아요!'.

acceptable.reason: Citing only the clearest evidence (she accepts Sunday) is reasonable; d adds that she names only the day, not the film.

steps.prompt: Your classmate 민수 invites you to eat out on Saturday, but you cannot go. Reply in Korean with 요-speech: do not say '싫어요', soften the refusal, and offer another day.

checks.label: names a different day/time than Saturday (일요일, 내일, 다음 ...)
softener or reason (좀, 죄송, 약속, 일이 있 ...)

selfAssess: Does my reply make clear that I cannot do Saturday?
Did I keep the friendship warm (softener, alternative)?
Would 민수 know what to do next?

modelAnswers.text: 죄송해요, 토요일은 좀 어려워요. 일요일은 어때요?
modelAnswers.note: Short and soft; uses 좀 and offers a day.

modelAnswers.text: 아, 토요일은 일이 있어서 어려울 것 같아요. 그럼 일요일에 만나요!
modelAnswers.note: Gives a reason instead of 좀, then proposes Sunday.

badAnswers.why: Direct, no softener, no alternative.
Drops the polite ending to a classmate you use 요 with, and offers no alternative.
Soft, but it offers no other day, so the plan is left hanging.

badAnswers.text: 미안, 토요일은 약속 있으니까 다음 주말에 보자.
badAnswers.why: Casual ending to a classmate you use 요 with.

steps.humanReview: Whether the tone feels warm and natural, and whether the reason given is believable and not rude, needs a person.
hints: Start by saying sorry or that it is a pity, then name Saturday.
Say sorry or give a short reason, then end with a question that proposes a different day.

rubric.full: Sees that Saturday (not the movie) is declined and cites the Sunday reply
rubric.partial: Sees a refusal but cannot say what exactly is refused
rubric.none: Reads it as agreement or misunderstanding

rubric.full: Polite, softened, alternative day offered
rubric.partial: Polite but blunt, or no alternative

alternatives: '다음 주말은 어때요?' also works as an alternative.
Using '-(으)ㄹ 것 같아요' instead of '좀' is equally soft.
hardCases: A learner who writes only '죄송해요' (an apology without a clear refusal) passes the polite check but the refusal is unclear.

cautions.language: Only simple 요-endings and day names; '좀' is explained through the chat rather than defined.
cautions.culture: Softened refusals with '좀…' are common in standard Korean, but how indirect people are varies. Honorific and politeness norms vary by region, workplace, age and personal preference; this task reflects common standard-Korean usage, not a rule for every situation.
cautions.accessibility: All material is text; emoji and any scene are described in words, nothing depends on colour. Romanization is not provided.

auto: Choice of the meaning and evidence
Polite ending, alternative day, softener present, no bare 싫어
human: Naturalness and warmth of the reply

subject: korean
title: Talking to a shop clerk
goal: Notice which customer lines are too casual for a stranger at a shop, decide why, and rewrite them politely.
thinking: Judging speech level against the relationship
Finding the lines that cause the problem
Rewriting for a different relationship
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks for the polite form of a given verb. Here you look at a real shop dialogue, decide which lines break the relationship, and explain why the clerk's polite speech does not allow casual speech back.
material: At a fruit shop. The clerk and the customer do not know each other. Both look like adults.

steps.prompt: One or more customer lines sound too casual for talking to a clerk you do not know. Pick one of them.
steps.explain: '얼마야?' and '줘' are 반말 (casual speech). Strangers normally use polite speech with each other: '얼마예요?' and '주세요'.
hints: Compare the customer's endings with the clerk's endings.
Look at the end of each customer line: do they end in -요/-습니다?

steps.prompt: The clerk uses polite speech (-요) to the customer. Can the customer answer in casual speech (반말) because of that?

options.text: No. Strangers use polite speech both ways; the clerk is polite as part of the job.
Yes. Both are adults talking, so casual speech is fine.
options.reveals: Being adults does not make casual speech fine; with a stranger the safe default is polite speech in both directions.

options.text: Yes. The customer is paying, so the customer decides.
options.reveals: Paying does not change the relationship. Customers also normally use polite speech.

options.text: No, but only because the clerk is much older.
options.reveals: Age can matter, but here age is not given. The main reason is that they are strangers.

steps.explain: The default between strangers is polite speech both ways. In shops, a clerk's polite speech is service language and gives the customer no right to use 반말.
hints: Ask: do the two people know each other?
Imagine the customer is a stranger on the bus. What speech level would you use?

steps.prompt: Rewrite the customer's two casual lines ('이 귤 얼마야?' and '그럼 두 봉지 줘.') so they fit this situation.

checks.label: asks the price politely (얼마예요, 얼마인가요, 가격 ...)
polite request or order (주세요, 살게요, 부탁 ...)
no casual 얼마야 / 줘 / 고마워 / 살게

selfAssess: Do both of my sentences end politely?
Would a clerk I do not know feel respected?

modelAnswers.text: 이 귤 얼마예요? 그럼 두 봉지 주세요.
이 귤 얼마예요? 그러면 두 봉지 주시겠어요?

badAnswers.text: 이 귤 얼마야? 두 봉지 줘.
badAnswers.why: Still casual speech.

badAnswers.text: 이 귤 얼마예요? 두 봉지 줘.
badAnswers.why: Only the first line was fixed.

steps.humanReview: Whether a learner's alternative wording (for example '두 봉지 주세요' vs '두 봉지 부탁드려요') is natural.
hints: Change the endings of both lines to a polite form.
Think of what you say when you order at a café.

rubric.full: Picks a casual line and explains the relationship (strangers)
rubric.partial: Picks a line but reason is vague
rubric.none: Picks a line that is fine

rubric.full: Both lines polite and natural

alternatives: '이거 얼마예요?' or '두 봉지 주세요' with or without 좀 are all fine.
Polite 해요체 and formal -습니다 are both acceptable here.
hardCases: Some older shopkeepers use 반말 to younger customers. That does not mean customers can do the same.

cautions.language: Very short sentences. The words 반말 and 존댓말 are glossed in the hints and explanation.
cautions.culture: Honorific and politeness norms vary by region, workplace, age and personal preference; this task reflects common standard-Korean usage, not a rule for every situation. Some shopkeepers speak casually to customers; the task treats polite speech as the safe default for a stranger.

subject: korean
title: Do the times match?
goal: Compare a short notice with a friend's text, notice that the times do not match, and ask a good clarifying question instead of agreeing.
thinking: Combining information from a notice and a message
Deciding what to ask before answering
Ruling out an irrelevant question
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks the time from one notice. Here two sources disagree, and you decide what is worth asking.
material:
Today is Friday, 10월 23일. Your school has a notice and your friend sent you a text.

[소풍 안내]
- 날짜: 10월 24일 토요일
- 장소: 한강공원
- 버스 출발: 아침 8시 30분 (학교 앞)
- 준비물: 도시락, 물, 편한 신발

친구 문자: "내일 7시에 학교 앞에서 만나요! 도시락 꼭 가져와요."

steps.prompt: Before you reply, which question is the most useful to ask your friend?

options.text: 버스는 내일 몇 시에 출발해요?
options.reveals: The notice already tells you the bus time, so this question does not add anything.

options.text: 버스 출발 시간이랑 만나는 시간이 왜 달라요?
도시락은 어디에서 사야 하는 거예요?
options.reveals: The text only says to bring a lunch box; where to buy it is not the puzzle.

options.text: 내일은 학교에서 소풍을 가는 날이에요?
options.reveals: The notice already confirms the picnic day.

options.text: 7시는 아침 7시예요, 저녁 7시예요?
options.reveals: Asking AM or PM can be a first step, but the bus leaves in the morning, so an evening meeting makes no sense. The real puzzle is the gap between the bus time and the meeting time.

steps.explain: The two sources differ (the notice says the bus leaves at 8:30, the text says to meet at 7:00). The best question points at the difference so the friend can explain.
hints: Find every time in the notice and in the text, then compare them.
Which question asks about something you do NOT already know from the notice?

acceptable.reason: Asking AM/PM is a reasonable first clarification, but it does not yet show that you noticed the 8:30 bus time.

steps.prompt: Write your question to your friend in Korean (friendly -요 speech). Mention both the bus time (or the notice) and the 7:00 meeting.

checks.label: mentions the bus or the 8:30 time

selfAssess: Does my question show that I noticed the two times are different?
Could my friend answer it with one short sentence?

modelAnswers.text: 버스는 8시 30분에 출발해요. 7시에 만나요?
7시요? 공지에는 버스가 8시 반이라고 되어 있는데, 왜 일찍 만나요?

badAnswers.why: Agrees without noticing the mismatch.
Asks something the notice already answers.

steps.humanReview: Whether the question is polite and clear for a friend; learners may mix register.
hints: Put the bus time and your friend's time side by side in one sentence.
End with a question word or -요?

rubric.full: Chooses and writes a question that contrasts 8:30 and 7:00
rubric.partial: Asks about time but not the contrast
rubric.none: Agrees or asks something already answered

rubric.full: Clear, friendly, mentions the times

alternatives: '혹시 7시 30분이에요?' also repairs the gap.
Asking '왜 일찍 만나요?' is also reasonable.
hardCases: Maybe the friend wants to meet before the bus on purpose; the task does not decide that.

cautions.language: Short notice with simple words; 소풍 and 준비물 appear in the notice only.
cautions.culture: School picnics are common; details vary. Honorific and politeness norms vary by region, workplace, age and personal preference; this task reflects common standard-Korean usage, not a rule for every situation.

subject: korean
title: Shopping with limits
goal: Turn a short text message with dropped words into precise limits, find several shopping baskets that satisfy them, and report one in Korean.
thinking: Inferring an omitted meaning (the limit)
Satisfying several constraints at once
Finding more than one solution
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks the price of one item. Here the message leaves things unsaid, and you must find several baskets that fit every condition.
prerequisites: Has met -까지 (up to), -보다 (than) and 이상 (this number or more); they are explained in the hints
material:
Your friend texts you before you go to the market:

"시장에 가요? 그럼 사과랑 귤 좀 사 와요. 만 원까지 쓸 수 있어요. 귤이 사과보다 많아야 해요. 모두 5봉지 이상이요."

[가격표]
사과 한 봉지: 2,000원
귤 한 봉지: 1,000원

steps.prompt: What does '만 원까지 쓸 수 있어요' tell you?

options.text: You may spend up to 10,000 won but not more.
You must spend exactly 10,000 won.
options.reveals: '까지' sets a limit, not an exact amount.

options.text: You must spend at least 10,000 won.
options.reveals: That would be the opposite: a minimum instead of a maximum.

options.text: One bag costs 10,000 won.
options.reveals: The prices are in the price list; 만 원 is the money you may use.

steps.explain: '-까지' marks an upper limit: up to 10,000 won, and spending less is fine.
hints: Think of '까지' as 'up to'.
Ask whether the friend would be unhappy if you spent 8,000 won.

steps.prompt: Find 3 baskets that fit every condition in the message, each with a different number of apple bags. a = bags of apples, g = bags of tangerines.

constraints.ok: You bought both apples and tangerines.
constraints.fail: The message asks for both 사과 and 귤 (at least one bag each).

constraints.ok: More tangerine bags than apple bags.
constraints.fail: 귤이 사과보다 많아야 해요: tangerine bags must be more than apple bags.
모두 5봉지 이상: at least 5 bags in total.

steps.explain: For example 1 apple + 4 tangerines = 6,000 won; 2 + 3 = 7,000 won; 3 + 4 = 10,000 won. Many baskets fit because the message gives limits, not one exact order.
hints: Write down the conditions in your own words first: '-보다 많아야 해요' = must be more than; '이상' = this number or more.
Try a = 1 and increase g until the total reaches 5 bags.
Check the money last: 2,000 × a + 1,000 × g, then change a.

because.prompt: Pick ONE of your baskets and send your friend a short text in Korean (polite -요) saying how many bags of each fruit you bought and the total.
selfAssess: Do the numbers in my text match one basket I built?
Is the total correct (2,000 × apples + 1,000 × tangerines)?

modelAnswers.text: 사과 2봉지랑 귤 3봉지를 샀어요. 모두 7,000원이에요.
사과는 한 봉지, 귤은 네 봉지 샀어요. 6천 원 썼어요.

badAnswers.why: Casual, no items, no numbers.
Does not say which fruit or how many.

because.humanReview: Whether the counts and the total in the text really match a valid basket (the checker only sees that numbers are present).
hints: Use one basket from above: which two numbers?
Say the apple count, the tangerine count, then the total in won.

rubric.full: Understands the limit and all conditions, builds valid baskets
Text names both fruits, numbers, polite

alternatives: Any basket that satisfies all five conditions is correct, e.g. (1, 5) or (2, 4).
A different but still polite report is fine.
hardCases: A learner may treat '귤이 사과보다 많아야 해요' as a wish; the task treats it as a condition because of '-아야 해요'.

cautions.language: Prices use digits; Korean number words appear only in the message.
cautions.culture: Market shopping for a friend is common; prices are made up.
cautions.accessibility: All material is text; emoji and any scene are described in words, nothing depends on colour. Romanization is not provided. The price list is written out as text.

auto: Each basket against the five conditions
The text has a polite ending, both fruits and a number
human: Whether the report matches the basket

subject: korean
title: What does the neighbour mean?
goal: Revise your reading of an indirect complaint as more of the conversation appears, then write a suitable note to the neighbour.
thinking: Inferring an indirect complaint
Revising an interpretation when more dialogue is revealed
Inferring a dropped possessor
Writing an apology and promise
differsFromPlain: Plain practice reads a complete dialogue once. Here the dialogue appears in parts and you must change your reading as it grows.
material: You live in apartment 302. An adult from apartment 202 (the floor below), whom you do not know well, stops you in the elevator.

steps.prompt: Read each part, choose the reading that seems most likely, then continue.
hints: Decide using only what you have read so far.
Look at the endings of the sentences (…, -서요, -는데) for what is left unsaid.
steps.reflect: Notice how a complaint can be built from small hints: first an unfinished sentence, then a reason, then a request. Politeness does not mean there is no request.

stages.info: 아래층 이웃: 안녕하세요, 위층 사시죠? 저녁에 가끔 쿵쿵 소리가 들려서요…

options.text: Making small talk about the building
Gently pointing out a noise problem
Asking you to move out
options.reveals: Nothing in the sentence suggests moving out; a neighbour who wanted that would be far more direct.

options.text: Inviting you to visit
options.reveals: There is no invitation language (like 놀러 오세요). The sentence is about sounds that bother the speaker.

stages.after: At this point both small talk and a hint at a problem are possible, but '들려서요…' ends with a reason and leaves the result unsaid, which often signals a complaint.

stages.info: 아래층 이웃: 아기가 9시쯤 자는데, 그때 소리가 나면 자꾸 깨서요.
stages.ask: Whose baby is it, and what does the neighbour hope?

options.text: Their own baby; they hope the evening noise will be reduced
Your baby; they want to help you
options.reveals: The baby is the one who wakes up because of the sound from above, so it belongs to the speaker, not to you.

options.text: Their own baby; they want you to move
options.reveals: The speaker's hope is about the noise, not about where you live; there is no sign they want you to move.

options.text: No one's baby; it is only small talk
options.reveals: The details about the baby (자는데, 깨서요) are a reason for a request, so this is more than small talk.

stages.after: The speaker drops the possessor, but the baby that wakes up because of the noise from above is the neighbour's. They hope for less noise, not that you leave.

stages.info:
나: 아, 죄송해요. 아이들이 저녁에 뛰어서요. 9시 이후에는 조심할게요.
아래층 이웃: 아니에요, 이해해 주셔서 감사해요. 9시 이후만 좀 부탁드려요.
stages.ask: What is the neighbour's attitude now?

options.text: Not angry; accepts your plan and asks for quiet after 9
Still very angry
options.reveals: '아니에요, 감사해요' is a calm, thankful tone, not an angry one.

options.text: Wants the children to stop running at all times
options.reveals: They ask only for after 9 ('9시 이후만'), not for no running at all times.

options.text: Does not care about the noise
options.reveals: They still say '부탁드려요', so quiet after 9 does matter to them.

stages.after: '아니에요, 감사해요' and '좀 부탁드려요' show a calm, polite request limited to after 9 p.m.

steps.prompt: The next day you leave a short note (쪽지) on the neighbour's door. Apologize, say what you will do, and thank them. Use polite speech.

checks.label: promise to change (조심, 조용히, 안 나게, 줄이 ...)

selfAssess: Is my promise concrete (a time or a behaviour)?
Would I be comfortable if a neighbour wrote this to me?
Did I thank them for telling me?

modelAnswers.text: 안녕하세요, 302호입니다. 어제 말씀해 주셔서 감사합니다. 시끄러워서 죄송합니다. 밤 9시 이후에는 아이들이 뛰지 않도록 조심하겠습니다.
202호 이웃분께. 소리 때문에 죄송해요. 저녁에는 더 조심할게요. 말씀해 주셔서 감사해요.

badAnswers.why: Casual, no apology or promise.

badAnswers.text: 아이들이 뛰는 건 어쩔 수 없어요. 이해해 주세요.
badAnswers.why: Polite but has no apology or promise to change.

steps.humanReview: Tone and sincerity of the apology; whether the promise is realistic.
hints: Start with your apartment number, then the apology.
Mention a time (like 9시 이후) or a behaviour you will change.

rubric.full: Moves from 'maybe small talk' to 'gentle request' as information arrives
rubric.partial: Correct at the end but cannot say what changed

rubric.full: Apology, concrete promise, thanks, polite

alternatives: At stage 1 both 'small talk' and 'hint at noise' are reasonable.
Either formal -습니다 or 해요체 is fine for the note.
hardCases: Some neighbours would be more direct; others would never mention the noise. The task shows only one common pattern.

cautions.language: Mixed levels of formality; -(으)ㄹ게요 and -아서/어서 appear.
cautions.culture: Noise between floors is a common topic in apartment buildings. Honorific and politeness norms vary by region, workplace, age and personal preference; this task reflects common standard-Korean usage, not a rule for every situation.
cautions.accessibility: All material is text; emoji and any scene are described in words, nothing depends on colour. Romanization is not provided.

Polite ending, apology and promise in the note
human: Sincerity and naturalness of the note

subject: korean
title: Can my friend get a refund?
goal: Combine a notice, a table and a friend's message to decide how much refund applies, point to the needed evidence, and explain it to the friend in Korean.
thinking: Combining notice, table and message
Choosing the relevant evidence
Explaining a conclusion with its reason
differsFromPlain: Plain practice reads a notice for one fact. Here the answer needs a comparison of a fraction rule with the friend's numbers, and then an explanation.
material:
[한국어 회화 수업 환불 안내]
수업은 총 8번(주 1회)입니다.

| 신청 시점 | 환불 |
| 수업 시작 전 | 전액 환불 |
| 전체 수업의 3분의 1이 지나기 전 | 3분의 2 환불 |
| 전체 수업의 절반이 지나기 전 | 절반 환불 |
| 절반이 지난 후 | 환불 불가 |

환불을 원하시면 수업이 없는 날 사무실에 오셔서 신청해 주세요.

친구 문자: "나 3번 들었는데 이번 주부터 일이 바빠서 못 가. 환불돼?"

steps.prompt: How much refund can your friend get?

options.text: Full refund
options.reveals: Full refund applies only before the course starts. Your friend has already attended 3 lessons.

options.text: Two-thirds refund
options.reveals: Two-thirds applies before one third of the lessons have passed. 3 of 8 is more than a third (about 2.7).

options.text: Half refund
No refund
options.reveals: No refund applies only after half (4 of 8) has passed. Your friend has had only 3.

steps.prompt: The conversation became awkward. Pick a line that is part of the cause: the phrase that can be read two ways, the reply that turns it into a plan, or the follow-up that pushes the plan again.
lines: 나: 네, 잘 지내요. 잘 지내시죠?

steps.explain: '언제 밥 한번 먹어요' (line 3) is often a friendly closing phrase, like 'let's get lunch sometime'. Line 4 treats it as a concrete plan and sets a date. options.reveals: The ending is formal, but the message is a bare statement: no apology, no regret and no softening ('안 갑니다' is a flat 'I am not going'), which is too blunt for a supervisor.

options.text: 아쉽지만 오늘은 개인 사정이 있어서 참석이 어렵습니다.

options.text: 오늘은 일정이 있어서 못 갈 것 같습니다. 다음에는 꼭 가겠습니다.
options.reveals: Suitable (reason, softener, promise about next time). It is not the only suitable one, so check the other options too.

steps.explain: a and c apologise or show regret ('죄송하지만', '아쉽지만'), give a reason and soften the refusal. d gives a reason, softens with '못 갈 것 같습니다' and promises next time. b only states a flat refusal ('안 갑니다') and so sounds blunt even though its ending is formal.
hints: For each message, note whether it apologises or shows regret, gives a reason, and softens with something like '-ㄹ 것 같습니다'.
Choose every message that does at least two of those things in a way a supervisor would accept.

acceptable.reason: Both are suitable; d also adds a next-time promise, so choosing all three is the fullest answer.
Both are suitable; c is also suitable.
Both are suitable; a is also suitable.

steps.prompt: Write your refusal to 팀장님. Use polite/formal speech, soften it, give a reason and mention the next time.

subject: korean
title: Who is doing it? Dropped subjects
goal: Work out who is meant in a chat where the subjects are dropped, find a line that stays ambiguous, and write your own short chat where a clue still shows who.
thinking: Inferring dropped subjects from honorific endings
Finding an ambiguous line
Making your own example
differsFromPlain: Plain practice marks the subject with -이/가. Here nothing is marked; you must use verb endings and context to know who does what, and then build your own example.
material:
수미 and 태호 work in the same office. They are trying to reach their 부장님 (department head). 비서 means the head's secretary.

수미: 부장님한테 전화했어요?
태호: 네, 했는데 안 받으세요.
수미: 비서한테는 물어봤어요?
태호: 네, 물어봤더니 지금 회의 중이시래요.

steps.prompt: In 태호's last line, who is in a meeting?

options.text: 부장님 (the department head)
태호
options.reveals: A speaker would not use the honorific ending -시- for himself.

options.text: 수미
options.reveals: 수미 is not the one being discussed; the honorific ending also points to someone higher.

options.text: 비서 (the secretary)
options.reveals: The secretary is the person who answered, not the person in the meeting.

steps.explain: '회의 중이시래요' contains the honorific -시-, which marks the subject as someone to be honoured: the 부장님.
hints: Look at the ending '이시-'.
Who in this chat deserves an honorific?

steps.prompt: Who told 태호 that?

options.text: The secretary (비서), the person 태호 asked
부장님 personally
options.reveals: 태호 asked the secretary, not the head, and the head is the one who is busy in the meeting.

options.text: 수미
options.reveals: 수미 is the person asking, not the one who answered.

options.text: It cannot be known
options.reveals: The earlier line '비서한테는 물어봤어요?' makes it clear.

steps.explain: '물어봤더니 ... -래요' = 'when I asked, (they) said that ...'. The person asked in the previous line is 비서.
hints: Find who 태호 asked in the line before.
Think about the pattern '-았/었더니'.

steps.prompt: In another chat, one line leaves it unclear who is meant, even though the verb is honorific, because two honoured people are in the conversation. Pick it.
steps.explain: '연락하신대요' has -시-, so the person is honoured, but both 사장님 and 팀장님 qualify and the earlier lines name them together. The reader cannot tell who will call again; adding the subject ('사장님이 ...' or '팀장님이 ...') fixes it.
hints: Find the people in the chat who would be spoken about with -시-.
In each line, ask whether the subject is named or can only be guessed.

steps.prompt: Make your own two-line chat in Korean (polite speech) from a school or work situation: someone asks what a teacher or boss said or did, and the answer drops the subject but an honorific ending still shows who.

checks.label: honorific ending in B's answer (-시-, -셨-, 세요 ...)
a plain greeting is not the honorific clue
B's answer drops the subject (no 'name + 이/께서')

selfAssess: Can a reader tell who did it without a subject?
Did I use an honorific only for the person who deserves it?

modelAnswers.text:
A: 선생님께서 뭐라고 하셨어요?
B: 내일까지 숙제를 내라고 하셨어요.
A: 부장님 오셨어요? B: 아니요, 아직 안 오셨어요. 곧 오신대요.
modelAnswers.note: Honorific verbs in answer; subject dropped.

badAnswers.text: A: 밥 먹었어요? B: 네, 먹었어요.
badAnswers.why: No honorific marker, so there is no clue about who.
Subject given; no question or honorific.

steps.humanReview: Whether the honorific is used for the right person and the chat is natural.
hints: Pick a person who deserves an honorific, like 선생님 or 부장님.
Ask with 뭐라고 하셨어요? or 오셨어요?

rubric.full: Identifies both subjects with the clue and the ambiguous line
Honorific used for the right person, a question, polite

alternatives: Context (who was asked before) can also fix the subject without an honorific.
A learner may use a short sentence like '네, 부장님이 오셨어요' with the subject; this is clear but loses the point.
hardCases: Honorific endings may also be used toward a customer or an elder who is not in the chat.
